sources.citation: Starbuck, C. J. Guttation: A Pressure Relief for Plants. University of Missouri IPM; published 2009-06-01, revised 2015-09-30.
sources.locator: Article paragraphs on leaf-margin droplets and nighttime conditions; web lines 29-52.
sources.observed_operation: Describes hydathode exudation at tips/margins when nighttime low transpiration and root pressure occur; high humidity, cool air and warm soil are favorable context.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: General extension explanation, not a crop-specific rule. Notes rare bacterial entry possibility, but droplets do not prove infection or explain pale leaves.
sources.applicability: Record droplet position and overnight/root-zone/environment conditions; cannot identify this case's droplets or cause.
sources.retrieval_operation: Opened the University of Missouri IPM page and inspected content and published/revised dates.

critic_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: General extension description; neither droplets nor the rare-entry note diagnose this unknown crop.
critic_evidence_check.applicability: Draft keeps guttation as one possible explanation and proposes recording droplet position/time and conditions.

sources.citation: Watson et al. Greenhouse Ventilation. UF/IFAS Extension publication AE-10/AE030; revision date not exposed.
sources.locator: Definitions/purpose; Winter Ventilation; Summer Ventilation; Spring–Fall Ventilation; Air Distribution (web lines 17-29, 44-70).
sources.observed_operation: Ventilation replaces inside air with outside air; mechanical and natural paths differ. Venting removes moisture, but winter heat demand rises; natural flow depends on vents, wind and thermal gradients.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Humidity examples include tomato leaf mold and seasonal guidance for specified contexts; not thresholds for unknown herbs. More ventilation can raise operating/heating cost.
sources.applicability: Frames climate-history and ventilation tradeoff; does not justify changing this house's schedule without local measurements.
sources.retrieval_operation: Opened the UF/IFAS page and reviewed cited sections.
sources.version: UF/IFAS publication AE-10/AE030; revision date not exposed on inspected live page.

critic_evidence_check.critic_locator: UF/IFAS AE-10/AE030 live page, lines 17-29 and 44-70.
critic_evidence_check.observed_operation: Defines ventilation as removal/replacement of greenhouse air; describes winter moisture-removal/heating tradeoff, summer heat control, natural vent dependence on wind/thermal gradients, and distribution limitations.
critic_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: Advice/examples are season- and system-dependent; tomato humidity examples are not herb-specific thresholds.
critic_evidence_check.applicability: Draft uses distinctions and tradeoffs without importing a setpoint; leaf condensation is explicitly an inference from general dew-point conditions.

sources.citation: Henderson, S., Gholami, D., Zheng, Y. Soil Moisture Sensor-based Systems are Suitable for Monitoring and Controlling Irrigation of Greenhouse Crops. HortScience 53(4), 552-559 (2018), DOI 10.21273/HORTSCI12676-17.
sources.locator: Abstract p.552; Methods pp.552-554; Results/Discussion pp.554-557; Conclusions p.557.
sources.observed_operation: Primary monitoring in southwestern Ontario commercial houses: ‘Genovese Gigante’ basil in peat mix/subirrigation and ‘Get Mee’ bellflower in a separate peat setup; 30/24 plants instrumented. Evaporation dishes across three layouts showed nonuniformity, with high/low ratios about 1.6–1.9; substrate VWC varied.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Observational monitoring did not prove irrigation caused growth differences; several VWC-growth correlations were absent. Sensor count/placement depends on local microclimate, crop and substrate.
sources.applicability: Supports positional mapping and distributed measurements; no established door effect or transferable trigger value.
sources.retrieval_operation: Opened HortScience PDF and inspected abstract, methods, results and conclusions. DOI: https://doi.org/10.21273/HORTSCI12676-17.
sources.version_and_identity_note: Henderson, S., Gholami, D., Zheng, Y. Soil Moisture Sensor-based Systems are Suitable for Monitoring and Controlling Irrigation of Greenhouse Crops. HortScience 53(4), 552-559 (2018), DOI 10.21273/HORTSCI12676-17.

critic_evidence_check.critic_locator: Exact carried ASHS PDF URL was opened but returned HTTP 403. Search result for the same ASHS primary paper returned article title, abstract, and methods excerpts; DOI 10.21273/HORTSCI12676-17.
critic_evidence_check.observed_operation: Primary article abstract reports ‘Genovese Gigante’ basil and ‘Get Mee’ bellflower in two commercial greenhouses, spatial microclimate/evaporation variation in three greenhouses, and large substrate-water variation. Returned methods excerpt reports Ontario houses and crop-specific controls (including heat at 17.5 °C and vents set for 20.5 °C; outside means differ between the crops).
critic_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: Excerpt is incomplete and the complete PDF could not be independently reopened; study did not establish a door effect or justify transfer of a trigger value.
critic_evidence_check.applicability: Supports only the draft’s bounded mapping/heterogeneity point. Climate and control details relevant to C-02 are available in the excerpt but omitted from the comparison.

reviser_evidence_check.access_utc_window: 2026-10-10T07:14:07Z–2026-10-10T07:16:49Z; individual request time not separately captured
reviser_evidence_check.locator: HortScience 53(4), pp. 552–554: Materials and Methods, bellflower and basil cultivation paragraphs, greenhouse A/B temperature and vent settings; greenhouse construction descriptions. Discussion on greenhouse age/control differences.
reviser_evidence_check.retrieval_operation: Retrieved the official ASHS PDF URL with curl and extracted text directly from the PDF with pdftotext. This independently verifies the climate/control details; no executable source code was run.
reviser_evidence_check.observed_operation: The bellflower ‘Get Mee’ trial in southwestern Ontario greenhouse A used 10.2 cm by 11.2 cm containers, a 78% peatmoss/22% perlite substrate and subirrigation; heat was maintained at 17.5 °C, vents set to open at 20.5 °C, and mean outside temperature was 4.8 °C. The basil ‘Genovese Gigante’ trial in greenhouse B used a peat-based mix and subirrigation under the same stated heat and vent settings, with mean outside temperature 14.1 °C. Greenhouse A was an early-2000s commercial house; B was built in 2015 and had more advanced climate-control systems; the positional evaporation assessment also included an older 1960s research greenhouse C. The article reports spatial evaporation and substrate-water variation, not a door effect or a causal fan/vent treatment.
reviser_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: These are study-specific production settings and outside conditions, not herb recommendations. Crop, substrate, greenhouse age/design, season, and production control differ from the unknown teaching bench. The article's observational comparisons do not establish the cause of this case's symptoms.
reviser_evidence_check.applicability: Adds the implementation differences needed to judge transfer; supports mapping and representative distributed measurements only.

sources.citation: Currey, C. J., Flax, N. J., Litvin, A. G., Metz, V. C. Substrate Volumetric Water Content Controls Growth and Development of Containerized Culinary Herbs. Agronomy 9(11), 667 (2019), DOI 10.3390/agronomy9110667.
sources.locator: Methods/Figs. 1-4; Results on sage, basil and dill; Discussion/Conclusions; PDF pp.2-10.
sources.observed_operation: Controlled greenhouse studies in basil, dill, parsley and sage, 11.4-cm pots, 75% peat/25% coarse perlite plus controlled-release fertilizer, sensor-controlled VWC 0.15–0.45 m³/m³ for four weeks. Growth responses differed by species/measure; irrigation and WUE responses were not uniform.
sources.governing_condition_default_exception: Specific substrate, pots, cultivars, fertilizer and four-week period; authors advise commercial trials under local crop and greenhouse conditions. No low-moisture safety guarantee for other crops.
sources.applicability: Direct culinary-herb evidence; keep crop identity, growth, water use and substrate state as separate endpoints.
sources.retrieval_operation: Opened primary MDPI PDF and inspected methods/results/conclusion. DOI landing-page open errored; PDF is reviewed artifact. DOI: https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4395/9/11/667.
sources.version_and_identity_note: Currey, C. J., Flax, N. J., Litvin, A. G., Metz, V. C. Substrate Volumetric Water Content Controls Growth and Development of Containerized Culinary Herbs. Agronomy 9(11), 667 (2019), DOI 10.3390/agronomy9110667.

critic_evidence_check.critic_locator: Publisher PDF at the exact source-map URL, Agronomy 9(11), 667 (2019): abstract/methods pp. 1–3; study outcomes/discussion in the remainder; published 2019-10-23.
critic_evidence_check.observed_operation: Basil, dill, parsley, and sage; 11.4 cm pots; 75% sphagnum peat/25% coarse perlite plus controlled-release fertilizer; VWC treatments 0.15–0.45 m3/m3; four weeks. Greenhouse was at Iowa State in a glass house with fog cooling, radiant hot-water floor/perimeter heating, environmental computer; day/night air targets 23/18 °C, with light/shade controls.
critic_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: Species/cultivars, medium, pot, fertility, greenhouse, and period are specific. Reduced VWC caused no visible damage in this setup but growth traits increased with VWC; this is not a safe target for an unknown crop.
critic_evidence_check.applicability: Supports keeping growth and water use separate and explicitly describing experimental climate/control context when discussing transfer.

reviser_evidence_check.locator: Agronomy 9(11), article 667 (2019), Materials and Methods, greenhouse and environmental-control description; PDF text around the greenhouse setup and treatment sections.
reviser_evidence_check.retrieval_operation: Retrieved the exact official MDPI static PDF URL in the inherited source record and extracted its text with pdftotext.
reviser_evidence_check.observed_operation: The four-week containerized herb study was conducted in a glass-glazed Iowa State greenhouse in Ames, Iowa, with fog cooling, radiant hot-water floor/perimeter heating, and an environmental computer. Day/night air setpoints were 23.0 ± 1 °C and 18.0 ± 1 °C; shade curtains were deployed above an outdoor-light threshold and high-pressure sodium lamps provided supplemental light. The study used basil, dill, parsley, and sage in 11.4 cm pots with 75% peat/25% coarse perlite and controlled-release fertilizer, under sensor-controlled VWC treatments.
reviser_evidence_check.governing_condition_default_exception: The greenhouse controls, crop/cultivars, substrate, pot size, fertilizer, and four-week duration are study-specific. No VWC treatment is a safe or recommended setting for this unknown crop.
reviser_evidence_check.applicability: Supports separate growth/water outcomes and explicit transfer limits; does not select a local irrigation target.
